clue.text: Sound chaps when it comes to calls

definitions.text: Sound chaps when it comes to calls

parts.words: Sound chaps when it comes to calls
parts.note: the men who sound the calls, as bugle and brass players sound fanfares and reveilles

explanation.surface: Praise for reliable fellows whenever a decision has to be made.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound' reads as 'dependable' and 'calls' as decisions; in fact these chaps sound calls on a brass instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Players of a brass instrument blow the calls of the military and the hunt.

clue.text: Little bird embracing old boy is booked

definitions.note: said of the name: it heads a book of the Apocrypha

indicators.note: embracing means holding inside, so the bird's letters go round the others

parts.note: a tit is a small songbird
OB stands for old boy, a former pupil

explanation.surface: A small bird holding a former pupil has a reservation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is booked' means 'has a book named after it': the Book of the old man Tobit is in the Apocrypha.
explanation.definitionFit: The Apocrypha contains a book named after this pious Israelite, so his name is a book title.

clue.text: From nude I emerge clothed!

indicators.note: emerge suggests the letters come out in a new form, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A naked person steps out fully dressed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'emerge' rearranges FROM NUDE I.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone wearing official dress is clothed in a standard outfit.

clue.text: The Gargery family has gone to pot

parts.note: Pip is brought up in the Gargery household in Dickens's Great Expectations
kin means family

explanation.surface: Dickens's blacksmith's household has gone to ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: In Great Expectations Pip is raised by his sister and Joe Gargery; 'gone to pot' reads as ruin, but pot is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A small earthenware cooking vessel is a kind of pot.

clue.text: T.T. managers can be terrible scolds

indicators.note: terrible suggests the letters are badly mangled, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Team bosses at the Isle of Man TT races can be fierce nags.
explanation.walkthrough: The TT is the Isle of Man motorcycle race; 'terrible' rearranges T.T. MANAGERS, 'can be' linking.
explanation.definitionFit: Overbearing, quarrelsome women are shrews who scold.

clue.text: "Who is here so. — that would not be a Roman?" (J. Caesar)

definitions.text: "Who is here so. — that would not be a Roman?" (J. Caesar)

parts.words: Who is here so. — that would not be a Roman?" (J. Caesar)
parts.note: the missing word in Brutus's speech in Julius Caesar meaning uncivilised or base

explanation.surface: A line from Brutus's funeral speech with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Brutus asks the crowd who is so barbarous that he would not be a Roman; supply the missing adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare uses the word for barbarous or uncivilised, unworthy of a citizen.

clue.text: Learning to make return for tax

annotationWithheld.why: Learning to make return for tax (4), answer SCOT: SCOT is an old word for a tax, but no parse makes 'Learning to make return' give the letters; the scan reads the same and no blog or database holds the clue
annotationWithheld.clue: Learning to make return for tax

clue.text: With Joshua he attained the milk and honey

definitions.text: With Joshua he attained the milk and honey

parts.words: With Joshua he attained the milk and honey
parts.note: of the spies Moses sent, only two reached the land of milk and honey

explanation.surface: A Bible companion reaches a land of plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: In Numbers only Joshua and this spy, of all who left Egypt as adults, entered Canaan, 'the land flowing with milk and honey'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible names this spy as the one, alongside Joshua, who lived to enter the Promised Land.

clue.text: Record of exploit that earns the accolade?

definitions.meaning: a legal document recording ownership of property
a deed earning a knighthood, the accolade being the tap of the sword

explanation.surface: A note of the feat that wins a knighthood.
explanation.walkthrough: The accolade is the tap on the shoulder that confers a knighthood, so a deed winning one earns a title.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal document proving ownership of land is one sense; a deed that wins a knighthood is the other.

clue.text: Where one is committed to polish up the image ?

parts.note: to rub something is to polish it
an icon is a sacred image

explanation.surface: Buff a religious picture until it shines.
explanation.walkthrough: Caesar crossed this river and committed himself to civil war, so to cross it is to pass the point of no return.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossing that Italian river was Caesar's irrevocable step, so it stands for any point of no return.

clue.text: Low flier of the old school?

definitions.text: Low flier of the old school?

parts.words: Low flier of the old school?
parts.note: a barrage balloon floats low over a city, and Colonel ..., the cartoon character, is a pompous old-school reactionary

explanation.surface: A dim pupil from a traditional school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low flier' sounds like a poor scholar; it is a tethered barrage balloon, and 'of the old school' is David Low's cartoon Colonel Blimp, a byword for British reactionaries.
explanation.definitionFit: A small non-rigid airship flies low, and the cartoon colonel of that name stands for diehard conservatism.

clue.text: Fishy type with a grey alternative?

definitions.text: Fishy type with a grey alternative?

parts.words: Fishy type with a grey alternative?
parts.note: a kind of fish whose name has a colour, alongside the grey species of the same family

explanation.surface: A shady character who has a dull understudy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fishy type' suggests a suspect person; it is literally a fish, and the grey mullet is a separate fish, so the red one is its alternative.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the red and the grey kinds are edible sea fish sold under the family name.

clue.text: Inappropriate kit for a Polar cit!

definitions.text: Inappropriate kit for a Polar cit!

indicators.note: inappropriate suggests the letters of the phrase are put in the wrong places, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Clothing unsuitable for someone living near the Pole.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inappropriate' rearranges POLAR CIT; the whole clue is also the definition, since hot-weather kit is wrong for a cit (city dweller) of the Arctic.
explanation.definitionFit: Lightweight clothes made for hot equatorial climates would be useless to an Arctic dweller.

clue.text: The stamp of quality

definitions.meaning: the French word for a postage stamp, used in philately
the distinctive character of a sound or voice

explanation.surface: A hallmark guaranteeing excellence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The stamp of quality' reads as a hallmark, but the answer is the French for a postage stamp and the musical term for tone colour.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is French for a postage stamp, and in music it names the tone colour of a voice or instrument.

clue.text: Arms-bearer frustrating to keyhole spies!

definitions.meaning: the shield on which a coat of arms is displayed
the pivoting plate that covers a keyhole

explanation.surface: Something armed that foils peeping toms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arms-bearer' sounds like a soldier, but means the heraldic shield; the same word names the plate covering a keyhole.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry it is the shield bearing arms; in joinery, the swinging cover that blocks a keyhole from prying eyes.

clue.text: It was just one round of pleasure for Kubla Khan !

definitions.text: It was just one round of pleasure for Kubla Khan !

parts.words: It was just one round of pleasure for Kubla Khan !
parts.note: in Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan decrees a stately pleasure building with a rounded roof

explanation.surface: The emperor's idea of fun was a single bout of enjoyment.
explanation.walkthrough: Coleridge's poem opens 'In Xanadu did Kubla Khan / A stately pleasure-dome decree'; 'round' describes the shape of the roof, not a bout.
explanation.definitionFit: A hemispherical roof is the rounded structure Coleridge's emperor ordered built.

clue.text: Flying elephant, though without skill, goes North for the Oaks

definitions.note: the answer precedes Oaks in the name of the Washington estate

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the elephant goes around the other piece

parts.note: Dumbo is Disney's flying elephant
art means skill

explanation.surface: A Disney elephant, though clumsy, heads north to the racecourse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of 'outside'. 'The Oaks' suggests the Epsom horse race, but it is Dumbarton Oaks, the estate in Washington.
explanation.definitionFit: Dumbarton Oaks is a historic estate in Washington DC, so the town's name completes that title.

clue.text: Schoolboy claims the trousers

definitions.meaning: British schoolboy slang 'I ... that' stakes a claim to something
loose-fitting trousers, as in Oxford ones

explanation.surface: A pupil says the trousers belong to him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags!' is British schoolboy slang for calling dibs; the same word means baggy trousers.
explanation.definitionFit: Children call out the word to stake first claim, and it is also slang for wide trousers such as Oxford ones.

clue.text: No pie, might one think ?

indicators.note: the question asks whether the words could be made into something else, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: Turning down dessert, would you say?
explanation.walkthrough: 'might one' asks whether NO PIE can be made into a new word, and it rearranges to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To express an opinion is to state what one believes.

clue.text: Heels over head in one account

parts.note: a version is one account of events

explanation.surface: Falling head over heels in someone's story.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition reverses 'head over heels', which is exactly what it describes: turning upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning something upside down, heels above head, is overturning its order.

clue.text: Places of concealment for record-holders ?

definitions.meaning: conjurers and cheats hide things up these
paper or card covers for gramophone records

explanation.surface: Where a champion stashes things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'record-holders' suggests champions, but means covers for vinyl records; the first sense is the arm parts of clothes where things are hidden.
explanation.definitionFit: Tricksters hide cards up the arms of a garment, and records are kept in card covers of the same name.

clue.text: It's ideal for 15 ac making a change at 50

indicators.note: change suggests the letters are rearranged into a new order

parts.note: the answer to 15 across is the rounded roof of Kubla Khan's palace
L is the Roman numeral for fifty

explanation.surface: Something perfect for a clue elsewhere that alters at the half-century.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making a change' rearranges DOME (15 across) with L (Roman fifty); 'at' joins the two.
explanation.definitionFit: A paragon is a perfect example to be copied, so it is an exemplary pattern.

clue.text: Soundly instructed not to get slack

indicators.note: soundly means by sound, so the word for the clue word is said aloud

parts.note: instructed means taught

explanation.surface: A pupil was firmly told not to slacken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly' looks like 'thoroughly' but signals that TAUGHT is heard as a word spelt differently.
explanation.definitionFit: A rope pulled tight is the opposite of loose, which keeps it from slackening.

clue.text: Greedy for a sixpence

parts.note: six is VI in Roman numerals
d was the abbreviation for a penny in old British money

explanation.surface: Wanting more for a small coin.
explanation.walkthrough: The sixpence was an old British coin; split it as VI (six) and D (old penny, from Latin denarius).
explanation.definitionFit: Someone eager and hungry for something wants it keenly.

clue.text: Sulky through lack of air ?

definitions.meaning: airless and close, as a stale room

explanation.surface: Moody because the room is stale.
explanation.walkthrough: The word means both huffy and close, as in a room without ventilation.
explanation.definitionFit: A huffy person and an airless, close room are both described by the word.

clue.text: In close harmony ?

parts.note: musically, voices singing close together; here people of one mind

explanation.surface: Singers keeping to tight harmony.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is barbershop singing; the answer describes people whose opinions match.
explanation.definitionFit: People who concur are of one opinion, in accord with each other.

clue.text: Keeping time, time, time, In a sort of — rhyme" (Poe)

definitions.text: Keeping time, time, time, In a sort of — rhyme" (Poe)

parts.words: Keeping time, time, time, In a sort of — rhyme" (Poe)
parts.note: the missing word in Poe's The Bells, describing the ancient Germanic alphabet's verse

explanation.surface: A line from Poe's poem The Bells with a word left out.
explanation.walkthrough: Poe's The Bells runs 'Keeping time, time, time, / In a sort of Runic rhyme'; supply the missing adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means relating to the ancient Germanic letters, used by Poe for an archaic incantatory rhyme.

clue.text: 6 gets off!

parts.note: taking 6 across as a tax, the phrase describes escaping payment, so going unpunished

explanation.surface: Someone from north of the border is acquitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 6 across (SCOT) is an old tax; to be free of it is to escape payment, and the phrase now means escaping without penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting away without penalty originally meant avoiding a tax of that old name.

clue.text: Bar for poets

indicators.note: for here means in place of, so the clue word's letters are used rearranged as a substitute

explanation.surface: A tavern for writers of verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub; it is the legal verb to bar, and 'for' signals rearranging POETS.
explanation.definitionFit: In law, to preclude someone from asserting something contrary to a previous position is to bar them.

clue.text: Theatrical row

parts.note: a raised row of seats in an auditorium, not a dramatic quarrel

explanation.surface: A melodramatic argument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' rhymes with 'cow' in the surface, a quarrel; it is a line of seats in a theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: Theatre seats are arranged in banked levels, one above another.

clue.text: Regent in a variety of orange

indicators.note: a variety is a different form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A ruling prince among different citrus types.
explanation.walkthrough: 'variety' rearranges REGENT IN A; 'of' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A mandarin type of citrus fruit is a small, loose-skinned kind of orange.

clue.text: Palm off low — class American priority?

indicators.note: a stage Brooklyn accent says the word with an oi sound, so the clue word is heard in that voice

parts.note: priority means first place

explanation.surface: Getting rid of a cheap American claim to precedence.
explanation.walkthrough: In stereotyped working-class New York speech 'first' is pronounced 'foist'; 'low-class American' tells you to hear the word that way.
explanation.definitionFit: To pass off something unwanted or fake onto someone is to impose it deceitfully.

clue.text: The Devil take it!

explanation.surface: An oath cursing something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Devil take it!' is an oath; split it as Old Nick, a name for Satan, and British slang for stealing.
explanation.definitionFit: Old Nick is a name for Satan, and in British slang the word means to steal.

clue.text: Spirit-photograph ?

parts.note: a liquor followed by a quick picture, read as a crisp ginger biscuit

explanation.surface: A photograph claiming to show a ghost.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'spirit photograph' claims to capture a ghost, but here spirit is a liquor and photograph a snapshot, together a crisp rolled biscuit.
explanation.definitionFit: The rolled ginger biscuit is named for the liquor and the quick snap of its texture.
